entry.author: Unitec
entry.summary:
In brief:

Around 70 current and former kaimahi ‘staff’, volunteers and community members gathered at Sanctuary Mahi Whenua, honouring more than 25 years of learning, environmental stewardship and community connection.

Established in 1999, the sanctuary was Auckland’s first multi-layered urban food forest, earning national and international recognition for its organic systems, biodiversity and sustainable land management.

The farewell acknowledged the site’s rich Māori and environmental history, celebrating the enduring relationships, knowledge and spirit of kaitiakitanga ‘guardianship.’

Close to seventy current and former kaimahi, alongside friends, volunteers and members of the wider community, gathered on Friday morning to farewell Sanctuary Mahi Whenua.

A special karakia acknowledging the site’s enduring legacy was led by Te Noho Kotahitanga Marae team, with Matua Hare Paniora, Taurahere Hohepa Renata and Kaihautū Rikona Andrews conducting a ceremonial blessing and hīkoi on the whenua.

The gathering recognised not only the significance of the land itself, but also the many relationships, memories and learnings that have grown there through decades of care, collaboration and kaitiakitanga.

Those who helped shape the sanctuary over the years shared reflections, including Trevor Crosby, chief spokesperson for the society that has served as guardians of the organic community ecosystem since 2017.

In 2007, twelve Māori gardening implements were uncovered on the site, including an adze that is now embedded in the floor in front of a carving in Ngākau Māhaki, preserving an important connection to the whenua and its history. The discovery was recorded by the New Zealand Archaeological Association.

Sanctuary Mahi Whenua was established between 1998 and 1999 by former kaimahi Brendan Hoare and Richard Main, working alongside horticulture students to create the gardens and food forest.

Over the following decade, the Unitec Hortecology Sanctuary Mahi Whenua gained regional, national and international recognition as a leading example of organic systems and sustainable urban land management.

In 2002, kaumātua Sir John Turei gifted the sanctuary its Māori name, Mahi Whenua. In 2004, it achieved organic certification and received a Gold Award in Auckland’s Create Your Own Eden competition.

Following the discontinuation of the horticulture programme in 2008, the site continued to serve the community through Workforce Auckland, supporting people with disabilities.

Established on the Mt Albert Campus in 1999, Sanctuary Mahi Whenua grew into a thriving urban food forest and biodiversity haven, home to more than 400 species of plants and trees.

It became a place where students, staff, volunteers and community members learned together, nurtured the environment and demonstrated what sustainable land stewardship could achieve in the heart of the city.

Technician Trina Smith says the sanctuary was Auckland’s first multi-layered urban food forest and one of the oldest of its kind in New Zealand.

“Having witnessed the Sanctuary Mahi Whenua emerge from an area of rank grass beside the conventional horticulture teaching beds that students, including myself, maintained, today’s farewell is particularly poignant,” Trina says.

“As a student, and later as a staff member and teacher, I have had the privilege of experiencing the Sanctuary from many perspectives over the years, including as a living classroom for my own students.

“As an ecologist, I especially valued the way the Sanctuary revealed the connections between soil, fungi, plants, insects, birds and people, demonstrating how healthy ecosystems are sustained through diversity and interdependence. It provided a unique place for students to learn directly from the land, building on a landscape with a long history of cultivation and food production.”

The whenua itself holds a much longer history. Before European settlement, its rich volcanic soils were cultivated by Māori.

From 2011, it became a community garden, with its rejuvenated food forest complementing the restoration of Ōakley Creek.

Although the land was sold to the Crown in 2018, the sanctuary’s story continued. In 2024, Sanctuary Mahi Whenua marked its 25th anniversary, celebrating a quarter-century of education, environmental stewardship and community connection.

“For 27 years, the Sanctuary fostered learning, connection and stewardship of the natural world. While it is deeply saddening to see this valuable learning resource lost, I remain hopeful that its legacy will endure through a new student-led garden nearby, where future generations can continue to learn from the rich relationships between people and nature that the Sanctuary so beautifully embodied,” says Trina.
